title: "Analysis Tools"
format: gfm

Offline tools are deliberately separate from live acquisition. Loading a file
or refreshing a frozen spectrum does not start, stop, clear, or reconfigure the
hardware measurement that produced it.

## MCA energy calibration

Open **Tools → MCA Energy Calibration...** after the MCA has collected a useful
spectrum. Select the channel and use **Replace with current spectrum** to copy a
stopped snapshot into the workspace. The calibration tool does not need to keep
the acquisition running.

To build a calibration:

1. Double-click each known full-energy peak to create a draggable reference
   seed. Place it near the intended peak; the seed itself is not used as the
   calibration coordinate.
2. Choose a centroid-fit half-width that contains the peak and enough local
   background without admitting unrelated structure. The default is 300 raw
   channels.
3. Enter a short label and the accepted reference energy in keV. Clear **Use**
   to exclude a questionable line without deleting it.
4. Inspect the fitted **Centroid ch.**, Gaussian-plus-linear-background curve,
   observed-minus-fit count residuals, and convergence state. A failed local
   fit blocks application instead of silently using the seed.
5. Select a **Linear** or **Quadratic** model. Two enabled references are the
   minimum for a linear fit and three are the minimum for a quadratic fit.
6. Inspect every value in the energy **Residual** column as well as the RMS and maximum
   residual below the table. Apply the result only after the point assignments
   and fit quality have been checked.

The residual for a line is `reference energy - fitted energy at its channel`.
A positive value means that the fitted curve predicts too little energy at that
point; a negative value means it predicts too much. A large or structured
residual can indicate a misplaced centroid, a wrongly identified line, pile-up,
gain drift, or a calibration model that is too simple.

A two-point linear calibration is exactly determined, so both residuals are
zero apart from floating-point rounding. That does **not** independently prove
linearity. Add a third or later verified line to test the linear model. The same
caution applies to a quadratic fit made from exactly three points.

### Live Na-22 generator example

The view below uses a stopped CH0 spectrum acquired by IIO histogram polling
on `192.168.10.135:30431`. A CAEN generator supplied artificial signals that
represent the Na-22 511 and 1274.537 keV lines; this was a functional software
test, not a radioactive-source or dose measurement. The run used negative
polarity, raw trigger `-512`, a 64 ns baseline, a 1024 ns window, and MCA
binning `128`. It accumulated 78,534 counts across the full two-line spectrum
without using or changing the PSU; the stopped MCA view reported zero energy
overranges.

Independent Gaussian-plus-linear-background fits placed the two generated
peak centroids at raw channels `609.114` and `5628.753`. Assigning those
positions to `511.000 keV` and `1274.537 keV` gives the illustrative linear
mapping

```text
energy [keV] = 418.34772 + 0.15210994 × MCA channel
```

![Applied MCA Energy Calibration on the live generator spectrum, showing the
seed and fitted-centroid columns, local Gaussian overlays, count residuals,
and the per-line energy residual table.](images/mca-energy-calibration-na22-live.png)

The displayed residuals are approximately zero because exactly two references
define this linear fit; the tiny values around `10^-13 keV` are numerical
rounding, not a measurement of detector linearity.

A spectrum copied while the MCA is running is labelled a live, non-atomic
snapshot. Applying calibration changes no FPGA register, bin, ROI, or raw
record. Raw channel remains the bottom axis and calibrated keV is added on the
top axis. Relevant DSP changes mark the calibration stale; power-of-two MCA
binning changes rescale coordinates without invalidating an otherwise matching
calibration.

Saved settings and later capture metadata retain reference points,
coefficients, residuals, and the energy-processing fingerprint.

Applying the calibration snaps each seed to its fitted centroid and shows the
local fit and count-residual overlays. Editing a point, spectrum, fit width, or
model hides those applied-fit overlays until the revised calibration is
applied. While any channel has a valid applied mapping, the persistent
**ENERGY CALIBRATED** status-bar badge lists the channels in its tooltip;
double-click it to reopen the calibration workspace.

After a valid fit, **Download report...** creates a new report directory rather
than overwriting an existing one. The two-page PDF and accompanying CSV/JSON
data preserve every copied spectrum, seed, fitted centroid and local curve,
count residual, calibration point, energy residual, setting, provenance field,
and the typeset centroid and energy-calibration equations.

## Peak-analysis workbench

Open **Tools → MCA Peak Analysis Workbench...**. It works on frozen copies of
live MCA spectra and also imports:

- ordinary or NLab CSV;
- Maestro/ORTEC-style `.Spe`;
- Tukan `.wdm`;
- CAEN calibrated `.txt3`;
- CAEN ROOT `Energy` histograms;
- validated ANSI/IEEE N42.42 `.n42` or `.xml`, including every spectrum in a
  multi-measurement document.

N42 import is offline and deterministic: the application uses bundled NIST
base and add-in schemas, disables external entities and external schema
resolution, ignores document schema-location hints, expands `CountedZeroes`,
and preserves instrument, detector, timing, measurement-class, and energy-
calibration metadata. Documents without a spectrum can be valid N42 but do not
create a workbench entry.

One to three Gaussian components can be combined with none, constant, linear,
centred exponential, error-function Compton-step, or logistic Fermi-step
backgrounds. Draggable markers seed and bound peak centres. Raw non-negative
counts use a Poisson-deviance fit; derived spectra use propagated variance.

Results include centroid, FWHM, area, resolution, uncertainty, reduced fit
statistic, AIC/BIC, component curves, residuals, and boundary/covariance
warnings. Spectrum arithmetic creates new immutable entries, requires matching
coordinate grids, propagates variance, and never interpolates silently.

The **Reference lines** tab uses the bundled, version-pinned NNDC ENSDF
catalogue without a network request. Select one or more parent nuclides and an
emission-probability threshold, or restrict candidates to lines inside the
explicit fit ROI. Candidate ranking and user-editable favourites are aids to
review, not isotope identification. Calibrated overlays are suppressed when the
selected spectrum has no valid energy mapping or its calibration is stale.

After a completed fit, **Download report...** writes a non-overwriting bundle
containing a branded two-page PDF, fit curve and components, residuals, peak and
parameter tables, fit statistics, provenance, the exact reference overlay, and
machine-readable CSV/JSON metadata.

The selected spectrum can also be exported as N42.42, and a completed fit can
be exported as a spectrum plus `SpectrumPeakAnalysisResults`. Export requires a
current energy calibration and positive real/live measurement times. It will
not invent an identity calibration or export stale calibration data. Known
digitizer endpoint/channel identity is retained; detector category, material,
and geometry remain `Other`/unspecified unless the source document explicitly
provided them.

### Fitting the generated 511 keV peak

The completed fit below uses the same stopped CH0 generator spectrum and the
linear calibration above:

1. Open **Tools → MCA Peak Analysis Workbench...** and copy the stopped MCA
   spectrum, or load an exported spectrum file.
2. Drag the shaded fit region around the 511 keV photopeak. This example uses
   raw channels `478.973–738.973`; avoid including unrelated peaks.
3. Select one Gaussian peak, a **Linear** background, and **Poisson deviance**
   for non-negative counting data.
4. Use **Suggest peak positions**, adjust the marker if necessary, then choose
   **Fit selected spectrum**.
5. Inspect the fitted curve, background component, residual trace, parameter
   uncertainties, reduced chi-square, and warnings together. A plausible
   centroid alone is not proof of a good model.

![MCA Peak Analysis Workbench Results tab after fitting the generated 511 keV
line with one Gaussian and a linear background.](images/mca-peak-fit-na22-511-live.png)

For this capture the fit returned raw centroid `608.961 ± 0.208` channels,
calibrated centroid `510.977 keV`, FWHM `42.406` channels (`6.450 keV`), and
resolution `1.262%`. The Poisson reduced chi-square was `1.078`, and the tool
reported no boundary or covariance warning.

These values describe this artificial generator signal, acquisition, selected
interval, model, and exactly determined two-point mapping. They are not a
detector-resolution measurement or an independent validation of Na-22 source
response. Recheck the background model, fit interval, residuals, gain
stability, and calibration references before using a fitted result
quantitatively.

## Dose calibration logger

Open **Tools -> Dose Calibration Logger...** to record detector response beside
a known source/setup and expected dose rate. Select one detector channel, enter
the reference fields, choose a new CSV path, and enable only the measurement
groups needed for the study. Reference edits become active only when editing
finishes, preventing a timer tick from recording a partially typed value.

Every row contains UTC and elapsed timestamps, the actual sample interval,
channel and source labels, and the committed dose value/unit. Optional groups
add:

- MCA count rate, pulse dead time, and acquisition elapsed time;
- non-negative total and visible-ROI counts added between accumulated MCA
  snapshots;
- HV/SiPM setpoints and available readbacks;
- detector, ADC, HAT, FPGA, and raw ADS5407 temperatures;
- cumulative PSD integrals above and below the current cut over both the full
  energy range and the selected PSD ROI.

The logger consumes already-polled snapshots and never starts acquisition or
adds hardware reads. The first MCA snapshot establishes the differential
baseline; unavailable data remain explicit blanks. Rows are flushed
immediately, existing files are never overwritten, and closing or rebuilding
the workspace closes the file cleanly. The adjacent plot can show any enabled
numeric column against elapsed time, but the CSV is the durable record.

Record source identity, geometry, shielding, stabilization time, detector
configuration, and the independent dose-reference instrument with the CSV.
The tool aligns those observations; it does not calculate or certify a final
dose conversion.

### Live logger functional example

The following capture uses live CH0 MCA snapshots from the same CAEN generator.
The expected dose is deliberately `0 µSv/h`, the setup label states that this
is a functional test with no PSU, and only MCA count-rate/dead-time and
differential-integral columns are enabled. Eight rows were recorded at 750 ms
intervals; the adjacent plot shows the live raw count rate. This demonstrates
CSV and plot behaviour only and must not be used as a dose calibration.

![Dose Calibration Logger after a live eight-row functional capture from the
CAEN Na-22 generator, with PSU and temperature columns disabled.](images/dose-calibration-na22-generator-live.png)

## PSD event readback

Open **Tools → PSD Event Readback...** to reconstruct energy/PSD matrices and
projections from:

- NLab NDMA v1/v2;
- CAEN CoMPASS or compatible legacy CAEN binaries;
- NLab HDF5;
- ROOT event trees.

The reader memory-maps binary files, slices HDF5, and iterates ROOT in chunks.
Memory therefore stays bounded by batch size rather than total file length.
CAEN PSD import requires raw Energy and Energy Short fields. Headerless
single-channel extracts are accepted only after conservative structural checks.

The current source path remains visible and its filename appears in the window
title. Set the energy ROI, fit ROI, and two centroid seeds, then choose **Fit
double Gaussian** for a bounded constant-background fit using Poisson-deviance
residuals. Review both centroids and FWHMs, the conventional
`|mu2 - mu1| / (FWHM1 + FWHM2)` figure of merit, reduced deviance, parameter
bounds, covariance, and convergence warning together. **Copy table** exports
the populations and shared diagnostics as tab-separated text.

After a qualified fit, **Download report...** creates a file-named directory
with a three-page PDF plus the full matrix, projections, cut-separated spectra,
fit components, settings, source/digitizer provenance, and JSON metadata. The
energy spectra follow the panel's linear/logarithmic selection. Sparse zero- and
one-count matrix bins are transparent for readability; exported counts are
unchanged.

## Waveform analysis and PSD reconstruction

Open **Tools → Waveform Analysis Workbench...** for native NLab Scope NDMA or
waveform-bearing CAEN CoMPASS data. NLab fixed frames are memory-mapped directly.
Variable-length CAEN files receive a background offset index, and only selected
frames are copied for display.

The workbench provides:

- median or mean baseline removal;
- automatic or explicit pulse polarity;
- draggable integration start, short-end, and long-end gates;
- `Qshort`, `Qlong`, and `(Qlong - Qshort) / Qlong`;
- energy-versus-ratio matrices and linked projections;
- event stride and maximum-event limits;
- debounced previews while gates are dragged;
- comparison with stored CAEN gate sums when available.

The energy projection ROI is preserved when gate changes rebuild the PSD
matrix. After a successful double-Gaussian fit, **Optimize gates** performs a
bounded, cancellable local search over the short- and long-gate endpoints while
holding the baseline, integration start, energy/fit ROIs, and centroid seeds
fixed. Candidates with poor convergence are excluded; the selected gates are
then applied to a complete rebuild and fit. Treat the result as a local optimum
for the selected data and constraints, not as a detector-independent setting.

Waveform report bundles include the same FOM diagnostics as PSD Event Readback
and additionally preserve the exact integration gates and processing context.
The current source path and filename remain visible throughout analysis and
report generation.

NLab Scope NDMA uses its known 8 ns stored-point period. CoMPASS waveform files
do not encode the ADC sample period; verify the operator-entered value for the
originating digitizer.

## MCA gain-drift diagnostic

Run `examples/mca_gain_drift_diagnostic.py` for a repeatable dual-channel trace
of a known photopeak during startup or thermal/bias settling. It restores the
host's saved MCA and ADC-temperature-correction configuration, starts fresh MCA
accumulations, and tracks both the differential-spectrum maximum and a local
centroid inside per-channel raw ROIs.

The diagnostic records MCA statistics, correction state, detector/board
temperatures, rails, clocks, standard board hwmon telemetry, power values, and
available HV feedback. It does not write Scope registers. PSU bias is
monitor-only unless `--apply-saved-psu` is supplied; that option applies saved
per-channel bias and guarantees safe shutdown cleanup, including on errors.
The original MCA state is restored after capture.

Outputs include time-series CSV, each differential ROI spectrum as compressed
NPZ, summary/configuration JSON/YAML, and early/late plus time-series PNG plots.
Keep an external supply's own log when it provides the detector bias. See the
command example and option details in the project
[README](https://github.com/nucliflare/nlab-digitizer-community#mca-startup-gain-drift-diagnostic).

## Two-channel timing validation

Use **Developer → Validate Two-Channel Timing...** with two native NLab MCA
files produced from one known pulse split between channels (lower channel in
A). The validator scans complete files for backwards timestamps, verifies time
overlap, and plots bounded nearest-neighbour delay samples.

A fixed channel-B offset in 8 ns steps can be saved in application settings and
YAML. Matching identity metadata or a narrow histogram does not prove shared
clock timing; verify against the known split-pulse setup. These nearest-neighbour
pairs are diagnostics, not coincidence counts.

## Coincidence matrices

The live Coincidence workspace produces prompt, delayed-random, and corrected
energy matrices, plus projections and timing diagnostics. Exported HDF5/ROOT
matrices preserve raw axes, gates, calibration metadata, and session state. See
[Coincidence Measurement](coincidence).

## Programmatic recipes

- [Scope Waveform Analysis](analyze_scope)
- [MCA List-Mode Analysis](analyze_listmode)

Use these recipes when automation is required. Prefer project readers over
hand-written binary offsets because they enforce current NDMA versions,
alignment, and bounded-memory behavior.
